fetched_contents.text: Void Content Minimization in Vacuum Infusion (VI) via Effective Degassing Abstract This paper addresses the major concern which component porosity represents in Vacuum Infusion (VI) manufacturing due to resin gelation at pressures close to absolute vacuum. Degassing is a fundamental step to minimize or even avoid resin outgassing and enhance dissolution of voids created during preform impregnation. The efficacy of different degassing procedures based on vacuum degassing, and assisted by adding a nucleation medium, High Speed (HS) resin stirring and/or later pressurization during different time intervals have been analyzed in terms of final void content is studied. Through a rigorous and careful design of the manufacturing process, outgassing effects on final void content were isolated from the rest of porosity causes and specimens with two clearly identifiable regions in terms of porosity were manufactured to facilitate its analysis. Maximum void content was kept under 4% and porous area size was reduced by 72% with respect to conventional vacuum degassing when resin was stirred at HS; therefore, highlighting the importance of enhancing bubble formation during degassing. Keywords: Fiber Reinforced Polymer (FRP), Vacuum Infusion (VI), degassing, porosity 1. Introduction Although Vacuum Infusion (VI) is a promising alternative to Resin Transfer Molding (RTM) and even prepreg manufacturing, it presents some drawbacks in terms of quality, such as lower fiber volume fraction, vf, and higher void volume fraction, v0 [1,2]. Void content, also referred to as porosity, is crucial in matrix performance. Mechanical properties of Fiber Reinforced Polymers (FRP) such as compression, inter-laminar shear and flexural strengths, and fatigue behavior are seriously affected by void content [3,4,5,6]. If porosity is extended to the surface, even surface finish of FRP components may be altered, deteriorating component aesthetics [7] and later bonding [8]. A previous paper presented a new VI process to which the current paper contributes with further studies [9]. The main causes of void formation in VI and RTM are resin flow through dual-scale heterogeneous porous media and outgassing of air dissolved into the resin. Both causes can be addressed by controlling processing conditions. Several studies are focused on predicting void formation in dual-scale porous media due to resin flow [10,11,12]; however, resin outgassing is not a common subject in FRP manufacturing research, even though it is a major concern in VI since resin is prone to outgas at pressures close to absolute vacuum due to its minimum air solubility, as stated by Henry’s law. Although final porosity depends on the whole manufacturing process and materials involved [13,14,15], resin outgassing may be reduced or even avoided by carrying out a proper resin degassing procedure before preform impregnation. Besides, resin capacity for dissolving voids formed during preform filling depends on the previous air concentration into the resin. Conventional degassing approaches applied in the FRP field consist of exposing a volume of resin to high vacuum levels for a specific amount of time. Nevertheless, the degassing efficacy of this procedure is questionable if the physics involved in the process is considered; since air is initially dispersed as molecules into the resin and molecules are removed very slowly from the solution through the resin free surface via diffusion. Vacuum degassing can be speeded up by creating bubbles which can be removed faster. Therefore, improving attempts are usually based on enhancing heterogeneous bubble nucleation by adding a nucleation medium or sparging [16,17]. Air molecules diffuse to bubbles, reaching a saturated solution, but are no longer over-saturated. However, some micro-bubbles may remain trapped near the resin surface after degassing; However, the combination of a nucleation medium and a system of capillary separation appears useful at filtrating these micro-bubbles [16]. A straight and reliable way of characterizing resin outgassing behavior in VI manufacturing remains challenging, since it not only depends on the quantity of dissolved air into the resin, but on manufacturing conditions and materials involved too. For example, Unifilo E-glass mat exhibits especially good bubble nucleation properties, enhancing resin outgassing [17]. In polymer manufacturing, in order to improve efficacy, degassing under vacuum pressures is often combined with auxiliary systems such as mixing, rotation, or sonication, which also help bubble formation through rupturing liquid polymers by cavitation [18]. In order to bridge the gap between VI and RTM in terms of component quality through minimizing void content, this paper explores the efficacy of conventional vacuum degassing, and the benefits of additional auxiliary systems which enhance bubble formation during degassing and dissolution of the remaining micro-bubbles in the volume of resin. Degassing effectiveness has been directly assessed by means of the resin outgassing behavior during VI manufacturing of glass-epoxy specimens, through the final specimen porosity content and after isolating outgassing effects from the rest of porosity causes. fetched_contents.text: Skip to content FacebookYouTube Previous Vacuum Infusion Process – Benefits, Dry Spots, Pinholes and More * View Larger Image This article shows the benefits of the Vacuum Infusion Process and how the possible pitfalls can be eliminated. “The Vacuum Infusion Process, or VIP for short is a composite process that offers the ability to create superior products out of fiber-reinforced plastics which are light in weight yet extremely strong.” The Vacuum Infusion Process uses the differential pressure between a closed mold system and the atmospheric pressure as driving force to push the resin into the lamination stack. The ratio between fiber to resin is significantly enhanced resulting in additional competitive advantages that aren’t available in the traditional hand lay-up or vacuum bagging technique for example. The closed mold process is also very clean. This results in less wasted resources and since epoxy allergy is still one of the evident dangers, minimal exposure to this material is desirable. The process starts with the dry reinforcement materials being placed on the mold’s surface. Specific types of flow media are then used to facilitate the resin flow. Tubing is inserted and a vacuum bag on top of the laminate is sealed on the molds perimeter – creating a closed mold system (CMS). Then a vacuum pump is used to evacuate the bagged system. The differential pressure between the low in-bag pressure and the higher atmospheric pressure than pushes the resin into the cavity and across the laminate. During this step the laminate is compacted, pushing the resin into the porous material until it is completely saturated. With the ability to drive the resin into the part during the process, a better distribution and yield ratio of fiber to resin is possible. Excess resin results in products that weigh more and are brittle. These drawbacks are eliminated with the Vacuum Infusion Process. In an industry and consumer market where lighter and stronger is better, the Vacuum Infusion Process is a proven and effective advantage in composite production leading to many enhancements over traditional methods. Benefits of the Vacuum Infusion Process (VIP) There are several benefits to the Vacuum Infusion Process over other traditional methods. Some of which have already been mentioned above. Below is a tentative list of benefits as to why you should be using Vacuum Resin Infusion rather than open mold techniques. * Stronger products because of better consolidation ratios and better bonding * Best Fiber to Volume Ratio * Thickness control * Lighter products * Reduced production costs (less wasted resin and errors) * Consistency (product quality can be controlled with greater certainty of perfection) * Low initial investment to get started * Environmentally friendly (reduced VOCs and HAPs, and better worker conditions as well) * Large projects possible (VIP aids the easy production of large structures – boat hulls, wind turbines and more) * No rushing for time constraints In making the decision to switch to VIP there will be some slight downtime in order to allow for the transition to Vacuum Resin Infusion. But that is quickly recouped with the benefits of the process over other techniques in the long-run. Most individuals are able to quickly learn the process. This makes the conversion an even more attractive option for composite production. “The ability to reduce skin contact and odors increases the safety of the production processes” Resin is cured inside a bagged system. This reduces fumes of volatile organic compounds and air pollutants. This can also result in greater employee morale and better overall company recognition and image for supporting environmental preservation efforts. Dry Spots in Vacuum Resin Infusion – How to Avoid We clearly realize the great advantages of the Vacuum Infusion Process in comparison to wet lay-up or wet lay-up and vacuum bagging. But there are still some wasteful areas caused by the standard VIP process consumables. By using a spiral wrap as the evacuation line, you run the risk of getting dry spots. When resin reaches the spiral wrap (the standard VIP evacuation line) it can easily been drawn out of the mold cavity since there is no barrier preventing that. The calculation of the resin flow path varies depending on certain parameters. E.g. the lamination stack is not homogeneous in terms of permeability. But resin runs faster through areas with less resistance compared to those with higher resistance. That increases the risk of producing dry areas which are not saturated by resin especially with more complex designed molds. Further down we learn how this can be avoided by using membrane technology. Pinholes in Vacuum Resin Infusion – How to Avoid With the standard vacuum resin infusion process the permanent existing vacuum drives the resin out of the laminate into the bleeder fabric and/or resin trap. That leads to voids in the surface caused by pinholes. Pinholes are tiny holes on the surface which are hard to fix and require post treatment, resulting in additional labor costs. This is particularly evident with visible carbon fiber parts. These parts are just clear coated and pinholes affect their post treatment costs tremendously. Also, to protect the vacuum pump from resin being sucked out of the mold system, the standard VIP has to apply a resin catch container or resin trap. “Above all, the permanent existing vacuum in the system is the driving force for potential embedded air bubbles. Introduction to VARTM Vacuum Assisted Resin Transfer Molding (VARTM) is a closed mold process that has revolutionized the manufacturing of fiber reinforced polymer (FRP) composite parts. This chapter introduces the basic concepts of VARTM, its historical development, and comparisons with other composite manufacturing processes. 1.1 Definition And Basic Concepts VARTM is a manufacturing process that combines the advantages of conventional resin transfer molding (RTM) with those of open mold hand layup processes. The process involves the following key elements: * A single-sided mold (usually an open mold) * Dry fiber reinforcement (preform) * Sealing the preform to the mold using a vacuum bag * Resin injection under vacuum pressure * Compaction using atmospheric pressure In VARTM, the pressure difference between ambient (atmospheric) pressure and vacuum pressure is used to compact the fiber preform and pull the resin into the mold. The Basics of Vacuum Resin Infusion Vacuum resin infusion is a highly efficient and precise method of manufacturing composite materials. It involves drawing a resin into a fiber mat in a mold through vacuum pressure. This process allows for a uniform distribution of the resin, ensuring consistent quality and integrity of the final product. The vacuum assists in compacting the fiber, eliminating air pockets and voids that can weaken the composite. Vacuum-assisted resin infusion takes this process a step further. It introduces an additional level of control over resin flow and curing. By carefully managing the vacuum pressure and the resin introduction rate, manufacturers can create complex shapes and large-scale parts with greater precision. This variant is particularly beneficial for high-performance applications where material consistency and strength are paramount. This guide breaks down the procedure, discussing the setup, materials needed, and the infusion process, ensuring clarity and efficiency for successful implementation. Setup and Preparation 1. Mold Preparation: Begin by preparing the mold that will shape the composite material. Ensure the mold surface is clean and apply a release agent to prevent the final product from sticking. 2. The peel ply ensures a better bonding surface for secondary processing, while the release film controls resin flow and prevents the vacuum bag from sticking to the resin. 4. Placement of Infusion Mesh and Vacuum Bag: Place an infusion mesh over the release film to help distribute resin evenly during infusion. Practical process implications and control strategies for vacuum infusion

Vacuum infusion is a closed-mold process in which vacuum pressure is used to drive resin into the fiber mat, compact the laminate, and improve fiber-to-resin control [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The most important process variables affecting resin distribution and consolidation are therefore the vacuum pressure itself, the resin flow path, the inlet/outlet arrangement, and the permeability or resistance of the fiber bed [N4-R5][N2-F2]. The cited material emphasizes that “the success of the resin infusion process relies on a proper choice of process parameters such as the positioning of inlet and outlet points, the ...” [N4-R5], which directly links process design to resin distribution.

Vacuum pressure is the primary driving force in vacuum infusion, and its setting and adjustment are central to the process. In the practical guide provided, the process starts by creating a vacuum by connecting the vacuum pump to the bag and turning it on, then checking for leaks to ensure a consistent vacuum level [N4-F4]. The same source describes the vacuum as a “differential pressure between a closed mold system and the atmospheric pressure” [N2-R1][N2-F2]. In practice, vacuum pressure is typically set and monitored through the vacuum pump and pressure gauge, with the goal of maintaining a balance between resin flow and void removal. The cited article also notes that lower vacuum pressure during infusion can reduce the propensity for problems, and that the goal in the inner bag is really only to drive resin into the cavity and across the laminate [N2-R2]. This implies that vacuum pressure is not set arbitrarily but is adjusted to match the resin flow requirements and the laminate geometry.

The main limitation on resin distribution is the flow path and the resistance it presents. The practical guide states that resin runs faster through areas with less resistance compared to those with higher resistance, increasing the risk of producing dry areas, especially in more complex molds [N2-F2]. This is consistent with the idea that resin distribution is limited by localized flow channels or permeability differences across the laminate. The cited material also notes that vacuum-assisted resin transfer molding (VARTM) relies on pressure gradients generated by pressure at gates or vacuum at outlets, or both [N3-R4], reinforcing that resin front propagation and saturation depend on the spatial variation of pressure across the preform.

The cited evidence also identifies several trade-offs between speed, quality, and process robustness. A lower vacuum pressure can reduce problems and improve process robustness, but may slow resin flow and increase the risk of dry spots [N2-R2]. Conversely, higher vacuum pressure can accelerate resin movement, but may create edge effects, race-tracking, or uneven filling [N3-R1]. The practical guide further notes that the vacuum-assisted process enables large composite parts of high quality at relatively low tooling costs, but also acknowledges potential outgassing and dry spot formation [N2-F2]. These trade-offs are especially important in practice: too low a vacuum may leave dry areas and underfill, while too high a vacuum may overfill or cause surface defects.

Overall, the most strongly affecting variables are vacuum pressure, inlet/outlet placement, resin flow media, and the laminate’s permeability and geometry [N4-R5][N2-F2][N3-R1]. Vacuum pressure is set and monitored through the vacuum pump and bag, with adjustments made to control resin flow and avoid voids or dry spots [N4-F4][N2-R2]. The trade-off is clear: increasing speed can reduce quality and robustness if resin distribution becomes uneven, while careful pressure control improves quality but may slow the process [N2-R2][N3-R1].

Vacuum pressure creates the driving force for resin flow through the fiber bed by generating a pressure gradient between the closed mold system and atmospheric pressure [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The practical guide explains that vacuum pressure pulls the resin into the cavity and across the laminate, compacting the fiber bed and improving resin distribution [N4-F4][N2-F2]. This is consistent with the broader vacuum-assisted resin transfer molding (VARTM) explanation, which notes that the pressure difference between ambient pressure and vacuum pressure is used to compact the fiber preform and pull the resin into the mold [N3-F3]. In other words, vacuum pressure is the primary motive force that enables resin to enter the fiber mat rather than relying on gravity alone.

Pressure gradients are central to how resin fronts propagate and saturation occurs. The cited VARTM explanation states that pressure drop along the flow path, edge effects, and race-tracking are key aspects of resin flow [N3-R1]. It also notes that through-thickness flow is the primary direction of resin flow, and that flow distribution media are used to facilitate even resin movement [N3-F3]. This means that resin saturation depends not just on the overall vacuum level, but on how pressure is distributed across the preform. The same source describes the resin flow by generalized Darcy’s law, where the pressure gradient ∇P drives the Darcy velocity u_D [N3-F3]. That formulation shows that the resin front moves faster where the pressure gradient is steeper, and saturation occurs when the resin has reached all the flow channels and the fiber bed is fully wetted.

The factors that limit resin distribution include flow channels, resin viscosity, and permeability. The practical guide notes that resin runs faster through areas with less resistance, increasing the risk of dry spots in complex molds [N2-F2]. This directly supports the idea that localized flow channels or low-resistance paths can cause uneven resin front propagation. The VARTM explanation also emphasizes permeability and fiber bundle flow as important factors, with dual-scale flow occurring between fiber bundles and within fiber bundles [N3-F3]. Additionally, resin viscosity is a major limiting factor, as the cited material states that resin viscosity affects flow behavior and filling time, and that it is usually modeled as a function of temperature and degree of cure [N3-F3]. This means that higher viscosity can slow resin penetration, especially in thick or highly packed laminates.

Taken together, vacuum pressure improves resin distribution by creating a differential pressure that drives resin into the fiber bed [N2-R1][N2-F2]. Pressure gradients then determine how the resin front propagates and how evenly the laminate becomes saturated [N3-R1][N3-F3]. The main limiting factors are localized flow paths, resin viscosity, and the permeability structure of the fiber bed [N2-F2][N3-F3].

## 1) How vacuum pressure improves resin distribution

Vacuum pressure improves resin distribution by creating the driving force for resin flow through the fiber bed. The pressure gradient generated by the vacuum pulls resin into the cavity and across the laminate, compacting the fiber bed and improving resin distribution [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The practical guide explains that vacuum pressure is used to compact the fiber, eliminate air pockets, and aid in resin flow [N4-F4][N2-F2]. In the broader vacuum-assisted resin transfer molding (VARTM) context, the pressure difference between ambient pressure and vacuum pressure is used to compact the fiber preform and pull the resin into the mold [N3-F3]. This means that vacuum pressure is not just a vacuum; it is the motive force that enables resin to move through the fiber bed.

Pressure gradients also determine how resin propagates and saturates the laminate. The cited VARTM explanation states that pressure drop along the flow path, edge effects, and race-tracking are key aspects of resin flow [N3-R1]. It also notes that through-thickness flow is the primary direction of resin flow, and that flow distribution media are used to facilitate even resin movement [N3-F3]. The same source describes resin flow by generalized Darcy’s law, where the pressure gradient ∇P drives the Darcy velocity u_D [N3-F3]. This formulation shows that the resin front moves faster where the pressure gradient is steeper, and saturation occurs when the resin has reached all the flow channels and the fiber bed is fully wetted. So, vacuum pressure does not just create a general flow; it creates a pressure field that guides resin movement and determines where saturation occurs.

Resin distribution is limited by several factors. The practical guide notes that resin runs faster through areas with less resistance, increasing the risk of dry spots in complex molds [N2-F2]. This supports the idea that localized flow channels or low-resistance paths can cause uneven resin front propagation. The VARTM explanation also emphasizes permeability and fiber bundle flow as important factors, with dual-scale flow occurring between fiber bundles and within fiber bundles [N3-F3]. Higher viscosity can slow resin penetration, especially in thick or highly packed laminates. So, the most important limitations to resin distribution are not only the vacuum level itself but also the local flow path, permeability, and resin viscosity.

## 4) Practical process implications and control strategies

The practical process implications show that vacuum pressure is the most important variable, but it is not set in isolation. The process is described as depending on a proper choice of process parameters such as the positioning of inlet and outlet points, and the cited material notes that the success of the resin infusion process relies on these choices [N4-R5]. In practice, vacuum pressure is set and monitored through the vacuum pump and pressure gauge, with the goal of maintaining a consistent vacuum level [N4-F4].
